content: The World Health Organization (WHO) will assess the likelihood and potential consequences of risks associated with the implementation of its snakebite envenoming strategy. Internal factors within WHO that could impact the strategy's execution will be evaluated, and measures will be implemented to address these challenges. Risks will be regularly assessed using validated tools to identify and mitigate external factors that may threaten the overall strategy or its individual components. Early identification and reduction or elimination of these risks will be prioritized. Regular consultations with partners and stakeholders will ensure a collaborative approach. WHO will employ a risk matrix to evaluate the probability of a risk occurring and the severity of its consequences. This matrix will guide the prioritization of risks, with the highest priority given to events that combine the greatest likelihood with the most significant impact. Continuous monitoring, consultation, and review will ensure that risks are managed effectively and strategically. WHO will work closely with partners and stakeholders to maintain the technical soundness of the strategy and achieve sustainable, long-term outcomes. Regular progress reviews and expert consultations will further enhance risk management. The budget for the snakebite envenoming strategy will increase incrementally as the program expands to include more countries. A significant portion of the budget will be allocated to country-level activities (54%) and regional coordination (17%). Prevention and control of snakebite envenoming will be integrated into broader national and sub-national health plans to maximize impact and reduce duplication. A detailed investment case will be prepared in the program's first year, and biannual budget reviews will ensure responsiveness to economic and other changes. During the pilot phase (2019–2020), $96 million will be allocated to strengthen health systems and communities in 10–12 countries where snakebite envenoming is a public health issue. Of this, $85 million will be used to assess the safety and efficacy of existing antivenoms, establish a trial antivenom stockpile for sub-Saharan Africa, and improve antivenom manufacturing and innovation. An additional $21 million will be allocated to enhance snakebite treatment from first aid to hospital discharge and reintegration into normal life. An economic model for supplying up to 500,000 effective antivenom treatments annually to sub-Saharan Africa will be developed, with additional funding sought from donors and governments. WHO will ensure that antivenoms and other treatments are safe, affordable, and accessible through a prequalification program and improved access to stockpiles. Monitoring and evaluation of activities will provide data for effective planning and review, ensuring the strategy remains responsive to changing circumstances. The midto long-term budget will be adjusted as needed to reflect global, regional, and national economic and geopolitical changes. The core goal of the strategy is to improve care for all snakebite patients, aiming to reduce deaths and disabilities by 50% by 2030. WHO’s work with communities and health systems in affected countries will contribute to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and universal health coverage. As the impact of investments becomes evident, a sustainable supply of effective antivenom products will be made available globally.
